title: Running a shared connection pool
scenario: One long section with five clear sub-topics, distilled into many small cards: a frame too large to read whole, which the renderer must split along its sub-topics without moving a caveat or an explanation away from its claim.
audience: Engineers joining the on-call rota of a service that shares a database
objective: Know how the pool is sized, timed out, health-checked, watched and recovered after a failover, with every limit next to the rule it qualifies.

sections.heading: Operating the pool › Sizing the pool
Operating the pool › Health checks and failover
Operating the pool › Watching the pool

units.quote: Opening a new database connection costs the Ledger service about 30 ms, because each one needs a TLS handshake and an authentication round trip.
A pool keeps a set of connections open and lends them to requests, so most requests skip that cost entirely.
The pool also caps how many connections the service can hold, which protects the database from a traffic spike.
Each Ledger instance runs a pool of at most 20 connections.

critical.note: The per-instance cap the rest of the sizing follows from.

units.quote: The database accepts 400 connections in total, and 40 of those are reserved for migrations and administrators.
That leaves room for 18 instances at full size, so the autoscaler is capped at 18 instances.

critical.note: The autoscaler cap that keeps the database within its connection limit.

units.quote: Raising the pool size only helps while requests are waiting for a connection; once the database CPU is saturated, more connections make every query slower.

critical.note: A bigger pool is not a general fix: past CPU saturation it makes things worse.

units.quote: A pool sized for peak traffic also holds idle connections at night, which costs memory on the database but nothing else.
A request waits at most 2 seconds to borrow a connection before it fails with `POOL_EXHAUSTED`.

critical.note: The wait limit and the error a caller sees.

units.quote: The wait limit is deliberately shorter than the 5-second request deadline, so the caller still has time to return a clear error.
Each query also has a statement timeout of 3 seconds, set with `SET statement_timeout = '3s'` when the connection is opened.
The statement timeout does not apply to migrations, which run on their own reserved connections without a limit.

critical.note: The exception to the statement timeout.

units.quote: A long transaction holds its connection for its whole duration, so the team keeps transactions under 500 ms.
Before lending a connection that has been idle for more than 60 seconds, the pool runs `SELECT 1` to check that it still works.
A connection that fails the check is closed and replaced, and the request gets a fresh one.
During a database failover, every open connection breaks at once, so the pool is drained and refilled from the new primary.
Refilling is limited to 5 new connections per second per instance, so that 18 instances reconnecting together don't overload the new primary.
Until the pool is refilled, requests may see `POOL_EXHAUSTED` errors for up to about 4 seconds.

critical.note: What callers see during a failover; the failover isn't invisible.

units.quote: A connection that stays borrowed for more than 10 seconds is logged as a possible leak, together with the stack trace of the code that borrowed it.
The pool does not take a leaked connection back by force, because the code holding it may still be using it.

critical.note: Detection only: a leak is logged, never reclaimed.

units.quote: Most leaks the team has found came from error paths that returned early without releasing the connection.
Leak warnings are reviewed every week, and a leak that comes back gets a ticket for the team that owns the code.
The pool exports three gauges: connections in use, idle connections, and requests waiting to borrow.
An alert pages the on-call engineer when requests have been waiting for more than 30 seconds in a row.
A sustained queue usually means slow queries rather than a pool that is too small, so the runbook starts with the slowest statements, not with the pool size.

critical.note: 'Usually' is a qualifier: slow queries are the likely cause, not the only one.

units.quote: The idle gauge drops to zero during a failover and recovers as the pool refills, which makes it a quick way to confirm that a failover has finished.
A pool makes connections cheap and bounded, but its size, its timeouts and its failover behaviour have to be set together with the database's own limits.

critical.note: The document's takeaway, with its own condition.

provenance.note: Original text written for this dataset. The Ledger service, every number (30 ms, 20/400/40/18 connections and instances, 2/3/5/4/10/30/60 seconds, 500 ms) and every identifier (POOL_EXHAUSTED, the statement_timeout setting) are invented for the example.
